lessons.title: Classes & objects
lessons.explain: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance built from it. __init__ runs at creation; self refers to the specific object.
objectives: Define a class and create instances from it
Explain how class changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect class with __init__ and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Forgetting `self` as the first parameter of an instance method, or confusing the class (blueprint) with an object (instance).

lessons.title: Inheritance
lessons.explain: A subclass reuses a parent's code and overrides what differs. super() calls the parent's version.
objectives: Reuse and extend a parent class's behavior in a subclass
Explain how inheritance changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect inheritance with super() and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Overriding a method entirely when you meant to extend it -- forgetting to call super() loses the parent's behavior.
lessons.explanation: A subclass reuses a parent's code and overrides what differs. super() calls the parent's version.

lessons.title: Polymorphism
lessons.explain: Same method name, different behavior. Code calling .area() works for any shape without type checks.
lessons.example: total = sum(s.area() for s in shapes)
objectives: Write code that works with any object implementing the expected interface
Explain how polymorphism changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect polymorphism with duck typing and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Adding explicit type-checks (isinstance chains) instead of relying on polymorphism to handle each type correctly.
lessons.explanation: Same method name, different behavior. Code calling .area() works for any shape without type checks.

lessons.title: Encapsulation
objectives: Bundle data and behavior together, and control access to internal state
Explain how encapsulation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect encapsulation with internal state and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Encapsulation means bundling data (attributes) and the methods that operate on it inside one class, while controlling what's exposed to the outside. A leading underscore (_balance) is Python's convention signaling 'internal, don't touch directly,' even though it's not strictly enforced.
commonMistakes: Exposing internal attributes directly and letting external code modify them freely, bypassing any validation the class's own methods would apply.
lessons.careerRelevance: Encapsulation is one of the four pillars of OOP and directly prevents a whole category of 'object got into an invalid state' bugs.

lessons.title: Abstraction
objectives: Expose only what's necessary, hiding implementation detail
Explain how abstraction changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect abstraction with abstract class and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Abstraction means exposing a simple interface while hiding the complex implementation behind it. When you call .sort() on a list, you don't need to know which sorting algorithm runs underneath -- that detail is abstracted away.
commonMistakes: Exposing every internal implementation detail through the public interface, forcing users of a class to understand its internals just to use it.
lessons.careerRelevance: Abstraction is what lets large codebases stay usable -- you can use a well-designed class without reading its internals.
lessons.explain: Abstraction means exposing a simple interface while hiding the complex implementation behind it. When you call .sort() on a list, you don't need to know which sorting algorithm runs underneath -- that detail is abstracted away.

lessons.title: Composition vs inheritance
objectives: Choose between 'is-a' inheritance and 'has-a' composition
Explain how composition changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect composition with is-a and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Inheritance models an 'is-a' relationship (a Dog IS-A Animal). Composition models a 'has-a' relationship (a Car HAS-A Engine) by holding an instance of another class as an attribute, rather than inheriting from it.
commonMistakes: Reaching for inheritance by default for every kind of code reuse, even when the relationship is really 'has-a' rather than 'is-a.'
lessons.careerRelevance: "Favor composition over inheritance" is one of the most repeated, real pieces of OOP design advice in professional codebases.
lessons.explain: Inheritance models an 'is-a' relationship (a Dog IS-A Animal). Composition models a 'has-a' relationship (a Car HAS-A Engine) by holding an instance of another class as an attribute, rather than inheriting from it.

lessons.title: SOLID principles: an overview
objectives: Recognize each of the five SOLID principles
Explain how SOLID changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect SOLID with single responsibility and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: SOLID is five design principles: Single Responsibility (a class should have one reason to change), Open/Closed (open for extension, closed for modification -- add new behavior without editing existing code), Liskov Substitution (a subclass should be usable anywhere its parent class is expected, without breaking things).
examples:
# Single Responsibility violated: a class that both saves to a database
# AND formats a report AND sends an email -- three reasons to change

# Dependency Inversion: a function that depends on an abstract 'Notifier'
# interface, not a concrete 'EmailSender' class directly -- swap implementations freely
commonMistakes: Treating SOLID as rigid rules to follow everywhere regardless of context, rather than principles that guide judgment about trade-offs.
lessons.careerRelevance: SOLID vocabulary is widely used in real code reviews and design discussions -- recognizing the terms is expected of an experienced engineer.
lessons.explain: SOLID is five design principles: Single Responsibility (a class should have one reason to change), Open/Closed (open for extension, closed for modification -- add new behavior without editing existing code), Liskov Substitution (a subclass should be usable anywhere its parent class is expected, without breaking things).

lessons.title: Design patterns: an introduction
objectives: Recognize a few common design patterns and what problem each solves
Explain how design pattern changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect design pattern with singleton and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A design pattern is a reusable, named solution to a recurring design problem. Singleton ensures a class has only one instance globally.
commonMistakes: Forcing a design pattern into code where it doesn't actually fit, just because it's a known pattern -- patterns solve specific problems, they're not universally 'better.'
lessons.careerRelevance: Recognizing common design patterns by name is a frequent, practical interview and code-review topic.
lessons.explain: A design pattern is a reusable, named solution to a recurring design problem. Singleton ensures a class has only one instance globally.

lessons.title: Interfaces & abstract classes in practice
objectives: Use abstract classes to enforce a shared contract across subclasses
Explain how abstract class changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect abstract class with contract and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An abstract class defines a contract -- methods every subclass MUST implement -- without providing (or only partially providing) the implementation itself. This lets you write code that works with ANY subclass polymorphically, as long as it fulfills the contract, without needing to know which specific subclass it is at runtime.
commonMistakes: Trying to instantiate an abstract class directly -- it's meant to be subclassed, not used on its own, and most languages enforce this.
lessons.careerRelevance: Programming against an interface/abstract contract, not a concrete class, is a foundational skill for writing flexible, testable code.

exercises.hint: composition (has-a) -- Car HAS an Engine, it isn't a kind of Engine

exercises.title: Spot a Single Responsibility violation
exercises.prompt: Given a class that saves data, formats reports, AND sends emails, explain which SOLID principle it violates and how to fix it.
exercises.hint: Single Responsibility -- split into three focused classes

exercises.title: Design with an abstract base class
exercises.prompt: Design an abstract 'Shape' class with an abstract area() method, then implement it for Circle and Square.

exercises.title: Diagnose a Liskov Substitution violation
exercises.prompt: A `Square` class inherits from `Rectangle` and overrides `set_width`/`set_height` so that setting one also changes the other (keeping it square). Code that works correctly with any `Rectangle` -- setting width and height independently and checking the resulting area -- breaks when passed a `Square`. Which SOLID principle's substitutability guarantee is being violated, and what's the real design fix?
exercises.hint: this violates the Liskov Substitution Principle -- a subclass should be usable anywhere its parent is expected without breaking correctness; the real fix isn't a special case for Square, it's recognizing that Square inheriting from Rectangle was the wrong relationship in the first place, since a Square doesn't actually behave like every Rectangle

exercises.title: Diagnose a broken subclass from a missing super().__init__()
exercises.prompt: A subclass defines its own `__init__` to add a new attribute, but forgets to call `super().__init__()`. Objects of this subclass are missing attributes the parent class was supposed to set up, causing errors later when parent methods try to use them. What went wrong, and what's the fix?
exercises.hint: overriding __init__ in a subclass completely replaces the parent's __init__ unless you explicitly call super().__init__(...) -- without it, none of the parent class's setup runs, so any attributes or state the parent was responsible for initializing simply don't exist

description: Model real systems with classes — encapsulation to composition.

interviewPreparation.q: What does it mean for a subclass to violate the Liskov Substitution Principle, with a concrete example?
interviewPreparation.a: It means code written to work correctly with the parent class breaks when given an instance of the subclass instead -- the classic example is Square inheriting from Rectangle: code that sets width and height independently and checks the resulting area works fine for any Rectangle, but breaks for Square, since setting one dimension unexpectedly changes the other.

interviewPreparation.q: When would you choose composition over inheritance?
interviewPreparation.a: When the relationship is genuinely 'has-a' rather than 'is-a' -- a Car has an Engine, but a Car isn't a kind of Engine. Composition also avoids the fragility of deep inheritance hierarchies, where a change to a base class can unpredictably affect many subclasses; favoring composition generally makes systems easier to change safely.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is forgetting super().__init__() in a subclass a real bug, not just a style issue?
interviewPreparation.a: Overriding __init__ completely replaces the parent's version unless you explicitly call super().__init__() -- so any state or setup the parent class was responsible for simply never happens, leading to missing attributes and confusing failures later when parent methods assume that setup occurred.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you decide if a class violates the Single Responsibility Principle?
interviewPreparation.a: Ask what would force this class to change -- if there are multiple unrelated reasons (a change to how data is saved, a change to report formatting, a change to email logic, all in the same class), it's doing too much. Each of those responsibilities changing independently is a sign they should be separate classes.

interviewPreparation.q: What's a practical benefit of designing to an interface or abstract base class, beyond satisfying a design principle?
interviewPreparation.a: It lets you swap implementations without changing the code that depends on them -- genuinely useful for testing (substituting a fake/mock implementation) and for extensibility (adding a new implementation later without touching existing code that already depends on the interface).

careerApplications: Interview topic on its own and the design basis of most production codebases.

capstone.title: Refactor a working-but-messy system into clean, SOLID-aligned design
capstone.description: Take a small system that technically works but has real design problems (a class doing too many unrelated things, inheritance used where composition would fit better, hardcoded dependencies that make testing hard) and refactor it applying SOLID principles deliberately -- not just because a checklist says to, but because you can explain what specific problem each change fixes. This capstone is about design judgment under a realistic 'this already works, don't break it' constraint, not designing a clean system from a blank page.
deliverables: A 'before' version with at least 2 genuine design problems (e.g. a class violating single responsibility, inheritance misused where composition fits better)
A refactored 'after' version, with a written explanation of exactly what problem each specific change fixes -- not just 'applied SOLID'
At least one interface or abstract base class enabling real polymorphic use (not just present for its own sake)
A test suite that still passes after refactoring, proving the refactor didn't silently change behavior
A short note on one thing you deliberately did NOT change, and why over-engineering it would have been worse than leaving it alone
capstone.portfolioTips: The 'before' and 'after' together, with a clear explanation of what each change actually fixes, is far more convincing than a clean greenfield design -- it's direct evidence you can improve real code under real constraints, which is most of what actual engineering work looks like.

industryUsage.usage: Java and Python style guides historically emphasize composition over inheritance and interface-driven design, reflecting exactly the kind of design judgment (not just syntax knowledge) this course builds.

SOLID principles and dependency inversion specifically underpin much of the design guidance in the .NET ecosystem, where testable, loosely-coupled class design is treated as a first-class engineering concern.
Maintaining large, long-lived codebases at scale makes design judgment (not reinventing every class from scratch, refactoring safely) a genuinely practical daily skill, not just an academic topic.
